newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech inflation downtrend seen continuing-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Czech inflation downtrend seen continuing-analysts.

text.p: Czech monthly inflation should quicken slightly in March but should not affect the current year-on-year downtrend which began in December, a Reuter survey of economists showed on Monday.

The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) is scheduled to release March CPI data on Tuesday at 0700 GMT, and most economists forecast an increase of about 0.4 percent month-on-month, up from 0.3 percent in February.

Since December the year-on-year rate has steadily dropped from 8.6 percent to 7.3 percent in February. The survey showed that a 0.4 percent month-on-month figure would put the year-on-year rate for March at about 7.1 percent.
"I don't think there will be any surprises in the March figure," said Boris Gomez of ING Barings in Prague.
"Something such as foodstuffs could have more of an effect than planned, but it is hard to predict this," he added.
Monthly inflation in March 1996 was 0.6 percent, putting the year-on-year rate at 8.9 percent.
If the predicted increase occurs, the annual average inflation rate would ease to 8.4 percent from 8.6 percent in Febraury.

"I think we will see inflation stay roughly at this level until July, then it will go up by maybe about two percentage points because of deregulation," said Vladimir Kreidl, an economist at Patria Finance.

In March the government approved proposals to raise household electricity prices by 15 percent, and rents at state-controlled housing by an average of 50 percent, effective July 1. Many Czechs still live in flats with artificially low rents and with energy bills subsidised by industrial users.
But whatever the CSU reports, analysts said they were sure of one thing -- the central bank is very unlikely to change its rates given its constant battle to keep inflation in check,
The Czech National Bank (CNB) raised its discount rate last June to 10.5 percent from 9.5 and the last-resort Lombard rate to 14 percent from 12.5 to help combat inflation.
In another move to tighten commercial banks' belts, the CNB also raised minimum reserve requirements to 11.5 percent of primary deposits from 8.5 percent as of August 1.
Central bank officials have said no rate cuts are in the works, and many analysts said that they saw little reason for the CNB to loosen its policy before mid-year at the earliest.
